subsection: 6. Increasing international involvement: the UN and the EEC

notes.b: Ireland's application to the UN was blocked for a decade by the Soviet Union, and it joined only in 1955 as part of a package deal.
points: Ireland applied for UN membership in 1946 and was blocked by Soviet vetoes for nearly a decade.
Ireland was admitted on 14 December 1955, together with 15 other states, in a settlement that ended the deadlock over membership.
Frank Aiken, Minister for External Affairs from 1951 to 1954 and again from 1957 to 1969, led the country's UN policy throughout the period.
Membership gave Ireland a platform outside the Commonwealth and a way to pursue independent foreign policy on international questions.

notes.h: Frank Aiken's independent line on disarmament
points: Aiken pressed for a UN resolution to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons to states that did not already have them, and he introduced the proposal in the late 1950s and early 1960s (verify exact dates).
The resolution was an early step in the non-proliferation treaty debate, and it was regarded as a practical measure by smaller states.
Ireland's stance on nuclear weapons put the country at odds with its Western partners on some issues, which Aiken's critics regarded as naive.

notes.b: Irish troops served in UN peacekeeping missions from 1960, which gave the country a practical role in international affairs.
points: Ireland sent troops to the Congo as part of the UN force from 1960, when the country had gained independence from Belgium and faced civil conflict.

Irish soldiers were involved in the fighting at Niemba in 1961 and at Jadotville in 1961, where the Irish company was besieged by Katangese forces (see the notes on the European decolonisation topic).
Irish forces were part of the UN peacekeeping force in Cyprus from 1964, sent to keep apart the Greek and Turkish communities after the outbreak of fighting.
Ireland contributed troops to the UN Interim Force in Lebanon from 1978, a force established in 1978 after Israeli operations in southern Lebanon.
Peacekeeping raised the profile of the Irish Defence Forces and gave Ireland a voice in UN debates on security questions.

notes.h: Boland and the UN General Assembly
points: Frederick Boland, Ireland's representative at the UN, was elected President of the UN General Assembly for its fifteenth session in 1960.
Boland's election was a sign of Ireland's respected role in the UN, given the country's small size and recent admission to the organisation.
Boland's period as President coincided with the Congo crisis, which dominated the Assembly's work at the time.

notes.h: The first EEC application and de Gaulle's veto, 1961–1963
points: Ireland applied to join the European Economic Community on 31 July 1961, the same day as Britain.
The applications were linked: Ireland's main export market was Britain, and Irish membership depended on British membership.
President Charles de Gaulle of France vetoed British membership in January 1963, which ended the negotiations for Ireland as well.
The veto meant that Ireland stayed outside the EEC until 1973, while the Lemass government continued to pursue free trade with Britain.

notes.h: The second application, negotiations and the 1972 referendum
points: Ireland applied again in 1967, along with Britain, Denmark and Norway, after Britain's second application.
Negotiations with the EEC opened in 1970 and produced agreed terms of entry in January 1972, including Ireland's place in the Common Agricultural Policy and its fisheries arrangements.
A referendum on EEC membership was held on 10 May 1972, and it passed with about 83 per cent of votes in favour (about, verify).
Ireland formally became a member of the European Communities on 1 January 1973, along with Britain and Denmark.

notes.h: The Single European Act and the Crotty case
points: The Single European Act was agreed by EEC member states in 1986 and aimed to complete the internal market by 1992.
In the Crotty case, the Irish Supreme Court ruled that ratifying the act required a constitutional referendum, because it transferred powers that the Constitution reserved to the state.
The Single European Act was approved by referendum in June 1987, and its passage confirmed that major EEC changes required the consent of Irish voters.

notes.h: Assessment: the UN or the EEC, which mattered more
points: The UN gave Ireland a platform for independent foreign policy and a practical role in peacekeeping, at a time when the state was small and outside the main alliances.
The EEC gave Ireland access to a large common market, and its membership brought large financial transfers through the Common Agricultural Policy and regional funds.
Contemporary view: many politicians saw the EEC as the decisive step towards modernising the economy, while others regarded UN membership as the more important sign of national independence.

Later view: historians tend to judge EEC membership as the more consequential change for the Irish economy and society, while the UN role is seen as an important but smaller part of Irish foreign policy.

keyTerms.definition: A group of countries that trade without internal tariffs and apply a common external tariff, which the EEC became in the 1960s.
The 1957 community of six states, later enlarged, which Ireland joined on 1 January 1973 as the European Communities.
The deployment of UN-authorised forces, usually lightly armed, to separate parties in conflict and to monitor ceasefires.
The effort to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons to states that did not already possess them.
The 1986 treaty that amended the founding treaties of the EEC to complete a single internal market by 1992.
The 1987 Supreme Court ruling that ratifying the Single European Act required a referendum, because it transferred constitutional powers.
